Abstract (124 word) 1 This study provides a heurisƟc model linking gross morphological features of compound eyes in 2

buterﬂies and moths and potenƟal visual funcƟons related to detectability, resoluƟon and 3

stereopsis. This framework, combined with empirical data from 2,730 specimens represenƟng 4

224 species widely sampled across a tribal level phylogeny of buterﬂies and a recent genomic 5

sampling of moths, supports the hypothesis that advantages of binocular vision select for 6

morphological architecture enhancing detectability in nocturnal species and stereopsis in 7

diurnal species. While these results are not enƟrely surprising given the diﬀerent light 8

environments that these species inhabit, our analysis also uncovered a strong correlaƟon 9

between eye size and interocular distance, parƟcularly in diurnal Lepidoptera. In general, males 10

have eyes that are more ventral facing than those of females, although this eﬀect is more 11

pronounced in some groups than others. Diurnal buterﬂies exhibit a striking phylogeneƟc 12

patern in the distribuƟon of dorsal- and ventral-facing eyes that deserves addiƟonal research. 13

Keywords: binocular vision, eye size, inter-eye distance, interocular distance, stereopsis, depth 14 percepƟon, diel acƟvity 15

Introduction 16 The diverse insect order Lepidoptera (buterﬂies and moths) contains species that exhibit 17

strikingly diﬀerent adult acƟvity paterns1, and depending on whether a species is day- or night- 18

ﬂying, adults tend to possess apposiƟon or superposiƟon type eyes, respecƟvely2-5. In 19

apposiƟon eyes, photons entering each cone are sent to a corresponding rhabdom, providing 20

beter resoluƟon and spaƟal registraƟon4,6,7 (Fig. 1a, c, & e). However, a photon-rich (bright) 21

environment is required to acƟvate the receptors8. SuperposiƟon eyes possess a clear zone 22

between the cone and receptor layers of the eye, which channels photons from mulƟple cones 23

to a single rhabdom2-4,6,7 (Fig. 1a, d, & f). This improves sensiƟvity to light (light detectability) 24

and facilitates beter performance by superposiƟon eyes in low-light condiƟons2-4. But 25

enhanced detecƟon comes at the cost of resoluƟon since the source of incoming photons 26

cannot be registered in space as accurately as in an apposiƟon eye7 (Fig. 1a & b). 27

While this trade-oﬀ is well understood, research on lepidopteran vision primarily focuses on 28

features of individual ommaƟdia, such as photon detecƟon and photoreceptors, opsins and 29


<!-- Page 5 -->


color vision, and ommaƟdia size and density for compound eyes9-25. Although visual ﬁeld has 30

been explored in detail in dragonﬂies26-28, it has rarely been menƟoned as a feature related to 31

binocular vision in Lepidoptera (but see 18,29,30). Here, we consider the role of binocularity and 32

its potenƟal contribuƟon to depth percepƟon (stereopsis) and detectability in lepidopteran eye 33

evoluƟon. For clarity, when we discuss the orientaƟon of the “eyes” of individual specimens, we 34

are referring collecƟvely to their two compound eyes, rather than to the many ommaƟdia that 35

make up each of those compound eyes. 36

Although binocular vision has been studied for more than a century31,32, research has focused 37

on vertebrates31-36. For terrestrial invertebrates, research on binocular vision has been 38

examined in bees37, dragonﬂies28,38,39 and praying manƟses40,41. AdapƟve advantages of 39

binocular vision39,42-47 include (1) improving detectability, (2) reducing the size of blind regions, 40

(3) seeing around obstacles, (4) generaƟng higher resoluƟon in the binocular visual ﬁeld, and (5) 41

aiding in depth percepƟon or stereopsis, which is criƟcal for visually hunƟng predators38-41. By 42

integraƟng depth percepƟon with funcƟonal goals of photon detecƟon and resoluƟon, the 43

following relaƟonships emerge: resoluƟon relies on detecƟon, and depth percepƟon is 44

generally as accurate as the minimal resoluƟon (Fig. 1b). Therefore, selecƟon for improved light 45

detectability in superposiƟon eyes not only comes at the cost of reduced spaƟal resoluƟon but 46

also reduced potenƟal for stereopsis, or depth percepƟon (Fig. 1d & f). 47

Eye size37,48, interocular distance40,49 (which we call ‘eye distance’ here for convenience), and 70

morphological traits interacƟvely inﬂuence visual traits, we assess the relaƟonship between 76

each pair of traits while staƟsƟcally controlling for the third (Materials and Methods). 77

Detailed features of ommaƟdia have been widely studied. The spherical shape52, density of 97

receptor lens15,52-54, corneal nipples23,52, and interreceptor angles15,51,53,54 inﬂuence the 98

formaƟon of local acute zones, where high spaƟal resoluƟon, high contrast, or high moƟon 99

detectability are specialized54. Within an ommaƟdium, photoreceptor alignment6,17, pigment 100

color6,17, and density of microvilli52 further facilitate the detecƟon of polarized light and target 101

wavelengths. In some special cases, species have compound eyes with apparent dorsoventral 102

separaƟon, typically associated with an unusual aspect of their life history. For example, a 103

genus of owlﬂies (Ascalaphus) have eyes that are divided into a large dorsal region and a 104

smaller ventral region55,56. Our model does not address these specializaƟons of compound eyes, 105

although we could conceivably predict circumstances where specializaƟon is more likely to 106

occur. Our primary focus here is to explore basic parameters of relaƟve size, shape and 107

posiƟoning of compound eyes across a broad spectrum of taxa in order to determine how these 108

can aﬀect visual funcƟons such as detectability, resoluƟon and stereopsis. 109

Based on our heurisƟc model (Materials and Methods), we hypothesize that if (1) detectability, 110

a funcƟonal goal, is important to a parƟcular species, selecƟon should favor morphological eye 111

traits that reduce the blind-spot range and enhance the binocular ﬁeld of view (Table 2). 112

Morphological traits that enhance binocular disparity may also be favored because this visual 113

trait is linearly correlated with the ability to see around obstacles when eye distance increases. 114

If (2) resoluƟon is especially important, selecƟon would favor morphologies that increase the 115

binocular ﬁeld of view because achieving beter resoluƟon from binocular vision requires 116

improving the degree of overlap in the ﬁeld of view (Table 2). If (3) stereopsis is important, 117

selecƟon should favor morphological traits that increase both binocular disparity and binocular 118


<!-- Page 10 -->


ﬁeld of view because these are the two visual funcƟons most strongly correlated with 119

stereopsis (Table 2). Thus, nocturnal species that generally have superposiƟon eyes are 120

predicted to have morphological eye traits that enhance detectability, reduce blind-spot range 121

and increase binocular ﬁeld of view. In this case, selecƟon may also favor morphological eye 122

traits that inﬂuence binocular disparity since this trait is also posiƟvely correlated with the 123

ability to see around obstacles, but we may not be able to disƟnguish the two (binocular 124

disparity and being able to see around obstacles) when we interpret the results. (Table 2). 125

Finally, we predict that selecƟon should favor stereopsis in diurnal species that generally have 126

apposiƟon eyes (Table 1), so morphological eye traits that increase both binocular disparity and 127

binocular ﬁeld of view should be favored (Table 2). 128

Results 162

The qualitative model 163 In our model, eye posiƟon was held constant when exploring the relaƟonship between eye size 164

and inter-eye distance (Fig. 2c & d). Binocular ﬁeld of view (BFOV) remains constant with 165

changing inter-eye distance but decreases with increasing eye size (Fig. 2c). Binocular disparity 166

(BD), a measure of depth percepƟon, is posiƟvely correlated with inter-eye distance. Smaller 167

blind-spot range (BSR) can be achieved through shorter inter-eye distance; having larger eye 168

size generally increases the BSR for a given eye distance. When we view all variables together in 169

a panel, large inter-eye distance can result in good binocular disparity, but it simultaneously 170

increases blind-spot range. If the evoluƟon of lepidopteran eye distance has undergone 171

selecƟon for both funcƟons (binocular disparity and blind-spot range), an opƟmal stable state 172


<!-- Page 13 -->


should underlie this tug of war (Fig. 2c). Our qualitaƟve model cannot predict the exact value of 173

the stable state, but we expect eye size to be posiƟvely correlated with eye distance around 174

this stable state (Fig. 2c). Thus, empirical evidence of a posiƟve correlaƟon between eye size 175

and eye distance with controlled eye posiƟon would suggest selecƟon on both binocular 176

disparity and blind-spot range (Fig. 2d (i)). A steeper slope indicates stronger selecƟon on blind- 177

spot range over binocular disparity (Fig. 2d (ii)). No signiﬁcant relaƟonship between eye size 178

and inter-eye distance observed in the empirical data would suggest that selecƟon intensity on 179

either blind-spot range or binocular disparity does not reach a threshold level, and an opƟmum 180

cannot be achieved (Fig. 2d (iii)). 181

For the eye size-posiƟon relaƟonship with eye distance held constant (Fig. 2e), we illustrate 182

only the dorsal facing examples; the ventral facing examples should show a roughly mirrored 183

patern. A more dorsal-facing eye posiƟon improves the binocular ﬁeld of view in the dorsal 184

region; the slope increases with decreasing eye size. Eye size shows no inﬂuence on binocular 185

disparity, but the binocular disparity on the dorsal side decreases for those taxa with more 186

dorsal-facing eye posiƟons. Blind-spot range on the dorsal side is smaller when the eyes face 187

more dorsally, and the inﬂuence of eye size on blind-spot range is exponenƟal, but with only 188

mild eﬀects on the dorsal side (Fig. 2e). 189

According to our qualitaƟve model, a stable state forms when the strength of two selecƟve 190

forces (binocular disparity versus the sum of the remaining two funcƟons [blind-spot range and 191

binocular ﬁeld of view]) are similar (Fig. 2e). We expect a negaƟve correlaƟon for species with 192

dorsal-facing eyes or a posiƟve correlaƟon for species with ventral-facing eyes (Fig. 2f (i)). 193

However, selecƟon for blind-spot range (BSR) and binocular ﬁeld of view (BFOV) cannot be 194

disƟnguished solely based on these results because both funcƟons are favored with increasing 195

degree of dorsal-facing eye posiƟon. Further funcƟonal evidence from individual ommaƟdia 196

within the compound eyes such as the distribuƟon of facet size, relaƟve localizaƟon of 197

pseudopupils, diﬀerent receptor types, presence of accessory pigments and eye shine (e. g. 60- 198

62) much of which can only be obtained from living buterﬂies, would be necessary to 199

disƟnguish selecƟon for these two funcƟons. When we observe no relaƟonship between eye 200

size and eye posiƟon within a group, either binocular disparity or the two other funcƟons 201

(blind-spot range and binocular ﬁeld of view) are likely to be under stronger selecƟon, so no 202

stable state is reached (Fig. 2f (ii)). 203

Discussion 278 The Lepidoptera are a group of insects with well-documented visually-guided behaviours, for 279

which there have been relaƟvely few comparaƟve studies thus far on the evoluƟon of key visual 280

morphological traits across a phylogeneƟc framework. The relaƟonship between eye size and 281

inter-eye distance (Fig. 4) might be expected due to allometric constraints and the strong 282

correlaƟon between these traits and body size: larger body size should be correlated with larger 283

eye size and inter-eye distance (Fig. 4a-b). However, our results surprisingly show that the 284

correlaƟon between eye size and inter-eye distance becomes much stronger aŌer controlling 285

for the eﬀect of body size (Fig. 4c & Fig. 5a-b). This reinforces the observaƟon that Lepidoptera 286

appear to be under strong selecƟon for visual traits including blind-spot range and binocular 287

disparity, with selecƟon favoring a reducƟon in blind-spot range in nocturnal species but an 288

increase in binocular disparity in diurnal species (Fig. 2d (i) & (ii)). 289

A signiﬁcant linear correlaƟon between eye size and posiƟon can only be detected in nocturnal 290

species (Fig. 5c), implying that binocular disparity, blind-spot range, and binocular ﬁeld of view 291

may approach a stable state (Fig. 2f (i)). Given that the strong correlaƟon between eye size and 292

distance indicates selecƟon for binocular disparity and blind-spot range (Fig. 2d (i)), binocular 293

ﬁeld of view is unlikely to also be under similarly strong selecƟon (Fig. 2f (i)), as the balance 294

between binocular disparity and blind-spot range would break if selecƟon for binocular ﬁeld of 295

view were equally strong (Fig. 2f (ii)). Thus, the relaƟvely weaker selecƟon on binocular ﬁeld of 296

view reduces but sƟll preserves the possibility of observing a signiﬁcant correlaƟon between 297

eye size and posiƟon in nocturnal species (Fig. 5c). These results jointly imply that for nocturnal 298

species, selecƟon for blind-spot range is stronger than selecƟon for binocular ﬁeld of view (Fig. 299

2d (i) & f (i)), and that selecƟon for binocular disparity is weaker than it is for diurnal species 300

(Fig. 2d (ii); Table 2). 301

Diurnal species show no detectable linear correlaƟon between eye size and eye posiƟon (Fig. 302

5c). This indicates that the selecƟon between binocular disparity, blind-spot range and 303


<!-- Page 21 -->


binocular ﬁeld of view does not approach a stable state (Fig. 2f (ii)). Given that the strong 304

correlaƟon between eye size and inter-eye distance indicates a stable state between binocular 305

disparity and blind-spot range (Fig. 5a, 2d (i) & (ii)), we can deduce that selecƟon for binocular 306

ﬁeld of view is strong enough to Ɵp the balance between binocular disparity and blind-spot 307

range in diurnal species (Fig. 2f (ii); Table 2) with either apposiƟon or superposiƟon eyes. 308

The traitgram (Fig. 5b) indicates that strong selecƟon on the relaƟonship between eye size and 309

inter-eye distance may have occurred aŌer the divergence of the buterﬂies at ~119 million 310

years ago. Though selecƟon between eye size and inter-eye distance may not have been 311

essenƟal for the evoluƟon of diurnal species, strong selecƟon is now observed in diurnal 312

buterﬂies and some diurnal moths, such as in Sphingidae (Bombycoidea), Uraniidae 313

(Geometroidea), and Castniidae (Sesioidea) (Fig. 5b). The eye size – posiƟon constraint is 314

signiﬁcant in most moths but appears to have diminished following the evoluƟon of the 315

buterﬂies (Fig. 5d). 316

We predicted that diurnal species, which generally have apposiƟon eyes, would be opƟmized 317

for stereopsis (Table 1), and that their eyes might therefore be under strong selecƟon for 318

binocular disparity and binocular ﬁeld of view (Table 2). The empirical results from diurnal 319

species support this hypothesis by showing that both binocular disparity and binocular ﬁeld of 320

view are strongly selected, with weaker (compared to nocturnal species) but sƟll detectable 321

selecƟon on blind-spot range. Hesperiids, despite possessing superposiƟon-type eyes, conform 322

to the observed patern and interpretaƟon seen in other diurnal Lepidoptera, suggesƟng the 323

possibility of having limited but funcƟonal stereopsis. We predicted that nocturnal species, 324

which generally have superposiƟon eyes, would be opƟmized for photon detecƟon (Table 1), 325

and that their eyes might therefore be under strong selecƟon for blind-spot range and 326

binocular ﬁeld of view (Table 2). The results of nocturnal species support this predicƟon, though 327

with room for debate, by showing strong selecƟon for blind-spot range and weaker selecƟon 328

for binocular ﬁeld of view and binocular disparity, the later of which is linearly correlated with 329

the ability to see around obstacles39,47. 330


<!-- Page 22 -->


Our ﬁnding that nocturnal lepidopterans typically exhibit more ventral-facing eye posiƟons 331

accords with research on rodents, where nocturnal species are more likely to have eyes facing 332

forward in the same direcƟon63,64. For rodents, the interpretaƟon of this characterisƟc is that 333

this eye posiƟon improves detectability under binocular summaƟon. This explanaƟon may also 334

hold for our results, where it appears that selecƟon favors detectability in nocturnal 335

Lepidoptera as a beneﬁt of binocular summaƟon39. However, dorsoventral eye posiƟon, 336

although studied in many other taxa, has rarely been explored in Lepidoptera, and speciﬁc 337

hypotheses and interpretaƟons of this characterisƟc based on more detailed analysis of the 338

internal anatomy of their eyes are scarce. 339

We can envision at least two main factors shaping the evoluƟon of eye posiƟon: the ﬁrst relates 340

to bioƟc factors, parƟcularly constraints on allocaƟon of resources to sensory organs located in 341

the head, and the second to abioƟc factors, such as the openness of the habitat that could 342

aﬀect light availability. For organ allocaƟon, we might predict a trade-oﬀ between antennal size 343

and eye size or posiƟon. Large antennae might block vision, and thus eyes might be expected to 344

move farther apart toward the ventral sides to compensate. Large antennae may also require 345

greater investment in the size of the deutocerebrum relaƟve to the protocerebrum, and if 346

overall brain size is constrained for any reason, this could generate a trade-oﬀ between 347

investment in diﬀerent neural architectures. This appears to be the case, for example, in 348

nocturnal and diurnal ﬁreﬂies, where selecƟon for mate detecƟon has resulted in nocturnal 349

species that rely more on light signals and have large eyes relaƟve to antennal size, and diurnal 350

species that invest more in pheromone producƟon and have large antennae relaƟve to eye 351

size65. For habitat openness, dorsal or ventral facing eyes could be helpful in diﬀerent 352

environments. Dorsal-facing eyes might help navigaƟon via polarized sky light66,67; this is more 353

likely to occur in open habitats, such as grasslands. Dorsal-facing eyes might also facilitate 354

object idenƟﬁcaƟon (including idenƟﬁcaƟon of conspeciﬁcs) in environments with complex 355

polarized light68, such as forest edges (intermediate openness). Ventral-facing eyes might assist 356

in locaƟng resources for both foraging and maƟng, and arguably might be equally helpful in all 357

habitats, regardless of openness. 358


<!-- Page 23 -->


Further analyses show no relaƟonship between eye posiƟon and antennal size, making organ 359

allocaƟon less likely as an explanaƟon (Fig. 6b). However, we found a strongly posiƟve 360

relaƟonship between relaƟve eye size and antennal size (r = 0.34, p <0.001), which concurs with 361

results from a study of Australian moths69. Eye posiƟon shows speciﬁcity in habitats with 362

diﬀerent degrees of openness, but these paterns diﬀer between nocturnal and diurnal species 363

(Fig. 6): Nocturnal species have eyes that are more ventral-facing regardless of habitat 364

openness, whereas diurnal species have more dorsal-facing eyes only in low-openness habitats 365

(i.e., forest) (Fig. 6c). This result does not fully match our predicƟons. Eye posiƟon may not be 366

correlated with habitat type in nocturnal species partly due to the more uniform light intensity 367

at night compared to during the day70,71. Forest and grassland habitats provide dramaƟcally 368

variable daylight environments, and this may have strongly aﬀected the evoluƟon of eye 369

posiƟon of diurnal species in diﬀerent habitat types. 370

Although our sample size is small, it is intriguing that Hedylidae (the “moth buterﬂies”) have 371

unusually dorsal-facing eye posiƟons among all buterﬂies (Papilionoidea). Also, the families 372

Papilionidae, Pieridae, and Riodinidae generally have more ventral-facing eye-posiƟons than 373

other groups, but include some striking outliers (Papilionidae: Pterourus glaucus, Parides 374

photinus, Zerynthia cerisyi; Pieridae: Colotis hetaera; Riodinidae: Sarota gamelia, Euselasia 375

euromus). Similarly, among the more dorsal-facing Nymphalidae, Lycaenidae and Hesperiidae, 376

both the Lycaenidae and Hesperiidae contain several striking outliers (Nymphalidae: Erebia 377

ligea; Lycaenidae: Iolaus sidus, Liphyra brassolis, Eumaeus atala; Hesperiidae: Heteropterus 378

morpheus, Ancistroides gemmifer). Further invesƟgaƟon of the behavior and life histories of 379

these outliers (and greater sampling in general) will hopefully shed light on possible adapƟve 380

advantages of diﬀerent eye posiƟons in diﬀerent habitats and for specialized species-speciﬁc 381

behaviours. 382

Male Lepidoptera are likely to have more ventral-facing eye posiƟons even when the 383

phylogenic paterns described above are taken into account (Fig. 7c). This might also be 384

associated with their behaviors and life histories. Male buterﬂies are known to patrol acƟvely 385

for females and/or conspeciﬁc pupae that are close to emergence (e.g. 72,73). Our results suggest 386

that males whose eyes are facing ventrally may therefore have beter binocular vision to be 387


<!-- Page 24 -->


able to ﬁnd mates and/or conspeciﬁc pupae. Studies have also pointed out that mate-locaƟng 388

behaviors depend in part on hostplant and habitat type74, and this might further explain why 389

the degree of sexual diﬀerence in eye posiƟon is correlated with the openness of the habitat 390

(Fig. 7e). Mixed habitats have relaƟvely diverse vegetaƟon compared to dense forests or open 391

grassland, and in these situaƟons, male perching strategies may not be as eﬀecƟve due to the 392

lack of obvious landmarks74. In these cases, other mate-locaƟng strategies such as patrolling 393

may be more eﬃcient. The degree of diﬀerence in eye posiƟon between males and females 394

varied in diﬀerent subgroups (diel acƟviƟes and habitats; Fig. 7d-e) and only represented a 395

trend when compared across the enƟre dataset (Fig. 7c), suggesƟng that sample size might be 396

contribuƟng to these eﬀects. Further research with an expanded dataset will help to resolve 397

these outstanding quesƟons. 398

In this study, we present a heurisƟc model that describes the gross morphological traits of 399

compound eyes and their relaƟonship to funcƟonal goals and daily acƟvity paterns of moths 400

and buterﬂies. Our ﬁndings indicate that the funcƟonal goals inferred from the model and our 401

ﬁndings from the empirical data converge with those paterns observed in some vertebrates 402

that have camera eyes. However, our understanding of the overall eye structure and visual 403

funcƟons of insects with compound eyes remains limited, and thus further invesƟgaƟon will be 404

necessary to ﬁnd ways to interpret and test some of the inferences proposed here. 405

Methods 406 Exemplar species were selected from a robust tribal-level phylogeny of buterﬂies58 and a well- 407

supported phylogeny of the “1KITE” Lepidoptera (buterﬂies and moths) based on 408

transcriptomes59. The 268 species in our iniƟal sample represented all families and >90% of the 409

described tribes of buterﬂies, and >50% of the species included in the family-level Lepidoptera 410

phylogeny59. Approximately six males and six females for each of the macro moths and 411

buterﬂies (a total of 3,094 specimens, Table S1) were imaged on both dorsal and ventral 412

sides75, and for illustraƟve purposes, a super phylogeny was constructed by integraƟng the 413

tribal-level phylogeny of buterﬂies and the family-level Lepidoptera phylogeny. 414

The eyes on each side of a specimen were manually segmented from the images using Adobe 415

Photoshop (Fig. 3a & b), followed by a systemaƟc analysis to derive the eye area and the 416

minimum distance between the two eyes (Fig. 3c). Some of the specimens had their heads 417

damaged or posiƟoned awkwardly so the eyes were covered by forelegs, proboscis, or labial 418

palps, and these individuals (N = 70 (2.3%); Table S3) were removed from the dataset. The 419

minimum eye distance of a set of dorsal and ventral images for each species were averaged as 420

the eye distance (Fig. 3c). The normalized diﬀerence between dorsal and ventral eye distances 421

was treated as the index for eye posiƟon, and posiƟve and negaƟve values represent dorsal and 422

ventral facing eyes, respecƟvely. The area of either a leŌ or right eye was derived as the sum of 423

dorsal + ventral images. This approach of esƟmaƟng eye area from data measured on only one 424

side (assuming bilateral symmetry and a roughly spherical shape of each compound eye) 425

enabled us to overcome situaƟons where mounted specimens had a rotated head that 426

obscured one side or the other. (Fig. 3c). 427

Body size was esƟmated from an ellipsoid based on the body length and width, using the 428

volume equaƟon: body size (cm3) = 4/3 π × body length (cm)/2 × (body width (cm)/2)2. To 429

miƟgate the inﬂuence of sampling bias in numbers of male and female specimens for each 430

species, male measurements and female measurements were calculated ﬁrst for a species, and 431

then averaged to derive a species-level dataset. The measurements were taken from all 432

specimens for those species that did not have specimens imaged for both sexes, or that did not 433

have informaƟon recorded regarding the sex of each specimen. Given that the eye 434

morphological data are highly sensiƟve to outliers, the species-level outliers were further 435

removed from the dataset (< 1% total variaƟon under two-tail staƟsƟcs; N = 24) before 436

staƟsƟcal analyses. Antennal size was esƟmated as the antennal area75 controlling for body 437

size. Of the original 268 species sampled, 224 (83.6%, including measurements from 2,500 438

individuals) had a suﬃcient number of replicates with intact compound eyes accessible for 439

measurements for this study. For the morphological measurements of compound eyes used in 440

these analyses, eye posiƟon was independent from body size and eye size was scored relaƟve 441

to body size. For analyses comparing sexual diﬀerences, only 168 species had suﬃcient 442


<!-- Page 26 -->


numbers of males and females to be retained in the dataset (specimens with unknown sex 443

were also excluded; Table S3). 444

Data on diel acƟvity paterns were scored for each species and eye types (apposiƟon or 445

superposiƟon) were inferred mainly from the published informaƟon20, with validaƟons for 446

specialized taxonomic groups such as Hedylidae25 (Table S2). Habitat descripƟons were drawn 447

The heurisƟc model includes three morphological traits (eye size, distance, and posiƟon) that 453

were measured for each species if available. These morphological traits inﬂuence essenƟal 454

regression. For example, when the relaƟonship between eye size and eye distance was 460

Both eye size and eye distance are highly correlated to body size (Fig. 4a), so the value of these 463
